documents.title: Annual Physical
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
ANNUAL PHYSICAL

53 y/o M. Interval: cirrhosis diagnosed by GI in August with ascites; since then drinking beer only, a few most nights. Feels better than last summer. Working full time.

Problems: alcoholic cirrhosis (ascites resolved clinically); chronic pancreatitis on Creon; aortoiliac occlusive disease (Leriche) on aspirin/statin; COPD; AUD severe; tobacco.

Meds: albuterol prn, ipratropium QID, Creon 36,000 with meals and snacks, omeprazole 20, aspirin 81, atorvastatin 40, thiamine 100, folic acid 1, MVI. NKDA.

ROS: morning cough as usual, no change. Claudication at about the same distance. Stools formed. No bleeding, no confusion. Sleeps OK.

Exam: Wt 86.5. Vitals in flowsheet. No icterus. Mouth and neck normal; no lymphadenopathy. Lungs with prolonged expiration, no crackles. Heart RRR, no murmur. Abdomen soft, nondistended, no fluid wave. Spider angiomas on chest. Femoral pulses faint. Feet cool, intact skin. No edema. Mood good.

AUDIT-C 7. PHQ-9 4.

A/P:
1. Health maintenance: Shingrix #2 today (series done). FIT kit given. Lung screening CT still never scheduled despite reminders; radiology will call him again and he promised to answer this time. Flu/COVID done in the fall.
2. Cirrhosis: CMP, CBC, INR, GGT today. GI follow-up due next month.
3. Lipids on atorvastatin today.
4. AUD: reduced but not stopped. Goal remains zero.
5. Tobacco: advised, declines.

RTC 3 months.

Outside Pulmonology Consultation
Date of service: 02/20/2024

Reason: persistent cough and weight loss.

Mr. Pelletier is 53, with COPD, ongoing tobacco use, chronic pancreatitis, alcoholic cirrhosis and Leriche syndrome. He reports three weeks of a cough that will not go away, with about ten pounds of weight loss. He has had no fevers, no night sweats and has not coughed up blood.

Family history: lung cancer in his father.
Social: current smoker, about 30 pack-years. Daily alcohol.
Meds: albuterol, ipratropium, aspirin, atorvastatin, Creon, omeprazole, thiamine, folic acid, multivitamin. NKDA.

Exam: afebrile. Respiratory rate 18, SpO2 94% on room air. Diminished breath sounds over the right upper lobe. No clubbing. No lymphadenopathy.

Chest radiograph today: 2 cm nodule in the right upper lobe.

Assessment: right upper lobe nodule in a heavy smoker, concerning for primary lung cancer.

Plan:
- CT chest this week.
- CT-guided biopsy to follow if the CT supports it.
- Oncology referral once tissue is obtained.

Pulmonology

Outside Procedure Note
Date of service: 02/27/2024
Procedure: CT-guided percutaneous biopsy, right upper lobe nodule (FNA and 20-gauge core x3).
Indication: 2 cm spiculated RUL nodule.
Technique: Prone, posterior approach, local lidocaine. Coaxial needle placed into the nodule under CT guidance.
Complications: none. Post-procedure CT without pneumothorax; 2-hour upright chest radiograph without pneumothorax. Discharged home.
Preliminary cytology: suspicious for malignancy. Final pathology to the ordering pulmonologist and PCP.

conditions.label: Non-small cell lung cancer, right upper lobe

reports.text:
ADDENDUM - CORE BIOPSY, RIGHT UPPER LOBE LUNG NODULE:
Infiltrating non-small cell carcinoma.
Immunohistochemistry: TTF-1 positive; p40 negative.
reports.conclusion: Non-small cell carcinoma, favor adenocarcinoma (TTF-1 positive, p40 negative).

documents.author: radiology
documents.body:
Outside Imaging Report
Exam: FDG PET-CT, skull base to mid-thigh. Date: 03/05/2024
Indication: Staging of biopsy-proven right upper lobe non-small cell carcinoma.
Findings: The 2 cm right upper lobe nodule is FDG avid, SUVmax 6.8. No FDG-avid hilar or mediastinal lymph nodes. No other pulmonary lesions. No abnormal uptake in the adrenals, liver or skeleton. Physiologic activity elsewhere. Pancreatic calcifications on the CT component.
Impression: FDG-avid right upper lobe primary without nodal or distant disease.

reports.text:
Full pulmonary function testing, pre-treatment evaluation.
FEV1 1.92 L (58% predicted). FEV1/FVC 0.57. Diffusing capacity (DLCO) 55% predicted. Acceptable and reproducible efforts.
reports.conclusion: Moderate airflow obstruction with reduced diffusing capacity, consistent with COPD.

documents.title: Thoracic Oncology Consultation
documents.author: oncology
documents.body:
Thoracic Oncology Consultation
Date of service: 03/07/2024

Diagnosis: non-small cell lung cancer of the right upper lobe, adenocarcinoma favored (TTF-1+, p40-), clinical stage IA2 (cT1b N0 M0).

History: 53-year-old foreman presenting with three weeks of cough and a 10-lb weight loss. CXR then CT showed a 2.0 cm spiculated RUL nodule. CT-guided biopsy 2/27: cytology suspicious, core confirms NSCLC. PET-CT 3/5: primary SUVmax 6.8, no nodal or distant uptake. PFTs 3/6: FEV1 1.92 L (58%), FEV1/FVC 0.57, DLCO 55%.

Comorbidities: alcoholic cirrhosis with prior ascites, chronic pancreatitis, aortoiliac occlusive disease, COPD. Current smoker (30 pack-years) and daily drinker.

Discussion: Lobectomy would be the standard approach for a fit patient. In his case, cirrhosis with prior decompensation and his lung function make surgery high risk. He was presented at our multidisciplinary thoracic tumor board on 3/7; the consensus recommendation is stereotactic body radiotherapy with curative intent. Referred to radiation oncology. No systemic therapy is indicated for this stage.

We discussed smoking cessation strongly; it matters for treatment outcome. He is thinking about it.

Follow-up: surveillance CT chest every 6 months after treatment, coordinated by radiation oncology.

Thoracic Oncology

Radiation Oncology Consultation
Date of service: 03/14/2024

Diagnosis: right upper lobe NSCLC, adenocarcinoma favored, cT1b N0 M0, stage IA2. Medically high risk for resection (cirrhosis, COPD with FEV1 58%).

The nodule is peripheral, away from the central airway. We recommend SBRT, 54 Gy in 3 fractions, every other day. Expected side effects reviewed: fatigue, chest wall soreness, cough, a small risk of radiation pneumonitis or rib fracture. Local control at this size is high.

CT simulation today. Treatment to begin 3/25.

documents.author: psychiatry
documents.body:
Outpatient Addiction Psychiatry - Initial Evaluation
Date of service: 08/22/2024
Referral: primary care, for alcohol use disorder in a patient with alcoholic cirrhosis.

He comes in tired, and says he has been feeling bloated a lot lately with some nausea now and then and less of an appetite. He denies abdominal pain, fever or yellowing. He has never had hepatitis and has not traveled.

Substance history: He describes his drinking as 'a few beers most evenings' and frames it as social, part of unwinding with the crew. Tobacco about a pack a day for 30 years. Denies any recreational drug use.

Mental status: cooperative, mildly defensive about drinking, mood 'fine,' affect appropriate, no suicidal ideation, no psychosis, cognition grossly intact.

Exam (limited): liver edge mildly enlarged on palpation. No ascites. I did not see stigmata of chronic liver disease.

Labs drawn before the visit: AST 94, ALT 48, total bilirubin 0.9, alkaline phosphatase 88, albumin 4.2, INR 1.0.

Diagnosis: alcohol use disorder, severe.

Plan:
- Motivational interviewing begun today; he is ambivalent but engaged.
- Referred to outpatient addiction counseling (group and individual).
- Acamprosate offered as a medication compatible with his liver disease; he declined for now.
- Return in 4 weeks.

Addiction Psychiatry

reports.conclusion: Enlarged heterogeneous liver without focal mass. Patent hepatic vasculature. No biliary obstruction.

documents.title: Gastroenterology Clinic Note
documents.author: gastroenterology
documents.body:
Outside Gastroenterology Clinic Note
Date of service: 02/17/2025

Mr. Pelletier, 54, with alcoholic cirrhosis and chronic pancreatitis, returns. When we last heard from his care team in August he had no jaundice. He now has fatigue, a poor appetite and abdominal discomfort. His wife has noticed his eyes turning yellow and that he is more irritable. He also mentions generalized muscle weakness and nausea at times, without vomiting or diarrhea. No trauma to the abdomen, no travel. He estimates he has lost about 6 kg (13 lb) over the past year without trying.

Family history: father died of a myocardial infarction at 63; mother died of breast cancer at 70.
Social: foreman, and calls the job stressful; says he unwinds with beer after work. Pressed, he acknowledges 8 to 10 beers a day for more than 25 years, plus whiskey on some weekends. A pack of cigarettes daily for 30 years. Eats mostly fast food and packaged snacks; little exercise.
ROS: some trouble sleeping, reduced libido, bruises easily at times. No vomiting of blood, black stools or rectal bleeding. No chest pain, palpitations or dyspnea.

Exam: T 37.0 C, BP 138/84, HR 88, RR 18. Fatigued but alert and oriented. Mild scleral icterus. Palmar erythema. Several spider angiomata over the upper chest and shoulders. Abdomen soft, mildly distended; liver edge firm and mildly tender, 3 cm below the right costal margin. No shifting dullness. Spleen not palpable. No edema.

Labs: AST 178, ALT 74, alkaline phosphatase 250, GGT elevated, total bilirubin 3.1. Albumin mildly low; INR mildly prolonged. Hepatitis B surface antigen and hepatitis C antibody negative.
Ultrasound today: enlarged liver with heterogeneous echotexture, no focal lesion, hepatic vessels patent.

Impression: alcoholic hepatitis on a background of alcoholic cirrhosis.

Plan:
- Percutaneous liver biopsy next week to assess inflammation and fibrosis.
- Complete abstinence; he was told this is now life-threatening.
- High-calorie, high-protein diet; continue Creon.
- Return after biopsy.

Gastroenterology

reports.text:
SPECIMEN: Liver, percutaneous core biopsy.
MICROSCOPIC: Hepatocytes show marked swelling with ballooning degeneration. Lobular inflammation rich in neutrophils. Many hepatocytes contain irregular, rope-like eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions (Mallory-Denk bodies).
reports.conclusion: Ballooning degeneration, neutrophilic inflammation and Mallory-Denk bodies, consistent with alcoholic hepatitis.
